qns_content.text: A concave mirror of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) from the mirror. What is the object distance?

text_solutions:
Focal length: \( f = -15 \, \text{cm} \) (concave mirror).

Image distance: \( v = -30 \, \text{cm} \) (real image, same side as object).

Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \).

\( \frac{1}{-30} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-15} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-15} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{-2 + 1}{30} = \frac{-1}{30} \).

\( u = -30 \, \text{cm} \).

qns_content.text: What is the primary condition under which a convex lens forms a virtual and magnified image?

options.text: Object between focal point and optical center

text_solutions: For a convex lens, a virtual and magnified image is formed when the object is placed between the focal point (F) and the optical center (O). In this position, the rays diverge after refraction, and their backward extensions converge on the same side as the object, producing a virtual, erect, and magnified image.

qns_content.text: A prism of angle \( 60^\circ \) and refractive index \( 1.45 \) produces what minimum deviation?
Why does a convex lens form a real image only when the object is outside the focal point?

options.text: Due to convergence on the opposite side

text_solutions: Outside the focal point, a convex lens converges rays to a point on the opposite side, forming a real image. Inside the focal point, rays diverge after refraction, appearing to come from a point on the same side, resulting in a virtual image instead.

qns_content.text: A convex lens of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the magnification?
What is the critical angle for a glass (\( n = 1.52 \)) to air interface?
In a concave mirror, when an object is placed beyond the center of curvature, what is the nature of the image formed?

text_solutions: For a concave mirror, if the object is placed beyond the center of curvature (C), the image is formed between the focal point (F) and C. The rays converge after reflection, producing a real image that is inverted and diminished in size compared to the object.

qns_content.text: A convex lens of focal length \( 25 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 50 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?
A convex lens has a power of \( +5 \, \text{D} \). What is its focal length in centimeters?
What is the critical angle for a water-air interface (\( n_{\text{water}} = 1.33 \))?
A prism of angle \( 60^\circ \) and refractive index \( 1.5 \) is placed in water (\( n = 1.33 \)). What is the new minimum deviation?
Why does the image formed by a convex lens become real and inverted when the object is moved beyond the focal point?

options.text: Due to convergence of rays on the opposite side

text_solutions: Beyond the focal point, a convex lens converges light rays to a point on the opposite side of the lens. This convergence forms a real image, and because the rays cross over, the image is inverted relative to the object’s orientation.

qns_content.text: A convex mirror of radius of curvature \( 40 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) behind the mirror. What is the object distance?
An object is placed \( 25 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of radius of curvature \( 40 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.5 \) has radii of curvature \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -12 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?
A prism of refracting angle \( 30^\circ \) and refractive index \( 1.6 \) produces what minimum deviation?
A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 4 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 25 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification?
Why can’t a concave mirror form an image at infinity when the object is placed at any finite distance?

text_solutions: A concave mirror converges reflected rays to a real focal point or diverges them to form a virtual image. For the image to be at infinity, the reflected rays must be parallel, which only occurs when the object is at the focal point, not at any finite distance beyond or before it.

qns_content.text: A ray of light passes from water (\( n = 1.33 \)) to air at an angle of incidence of \( 49^\circ \). What happens?

text_solutions:
Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{1}{1.33} \approx 0.752 \Rightarrow i_c \approx 48.75^\circ \).

Since \( i = 49^\circ > i_c \), total internal reflection occurs.

qns_content.text: A prism of angle \( 45^\circ \) has a refractive index of \( 1.6 \). What is the angle of minimum deviation?
An object is placed \( 14 \, \text{cm} \) from a convex mirror of focal length \( 28 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification?
A convex mirror of focal length \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) behind the mirror. What is the object distance?
A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at infinity. What is the magnification?
Why does a plane mirror not produce magnification greater than unity?

text_solutions: A plane mirror reflects light such that the image distance equals the object distance, and the image is formed by direct reflection without convergence or divergence. This results in an image of the same size as the object, with a magnification of 1, as there’s no mechanism to alter the apparent size.

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 2.5 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 20 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?

text_solutions:
Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{20}{2.5} = 8 \).

Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{5} = 5 \).

Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 8 \times 5 = 40 \).

Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 8 \times 6.25 = 50 \).

qns_content.text: A convex lens of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?

A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 100 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
In a reflecting telescope, why is a concave mirror preferred over a convex lens as the objective?

text_solutions: A concave mirror avoids chromatic aberration (color distortion) that occurs in lenses due to different wavelengths refracting differently. Mirrors reflect all wavelengths uniformly, providing clearer images, and are easier to support mechanically for large apertures, enhancing light-gathering power.

qns_content.text: A converging beam meets a concave lens (\( f = 10 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 4 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 1.2 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 18 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?

text_solutions:
Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{18}{1.2} = 15 \).

Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{6} \approx 4.17 \).

Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 15 \times 4.17 \approx 62.55 \approx 63 \).

qns_content.text: What happens to the power of a convex lens when its surrounding medium’s refractive index increases?

text_solutions: The power of a convex lens (P = 1/f) decreases as the surrounding medium’s refractive index increases. This is because the focal length increases due to a reduced difference in refractive indices between the lens and the medium, lowering the lens’s ability to converge light.

qns_content.text: A ray of light passes from air (\( n = 1 \)) to dense flint glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 45^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
What is the critical angle for a water (\( n = 1.33 \)) to air interface?
In a prism, what causes the emergent ray to deviate from the incident ray’s path?

text_solutions: The deviation in a prism occurs because light refracts at both the entry and exit faces, bending toward the normal when entering (denser medium) and away from the normal when exiting (rarer medium). The prism’s geometry and refractive index determine the total deviation angle.

qns_content.text: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 2 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 18 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?

text_solutions:
Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{18}{2} = 9 \).

Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{5} = 5 \).

Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 9 \times 5 = 45 \).

qns_content.text: A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 4 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at infinity. What is the magnification?
A coin lies at the bottom of a water tank (\( n = 1.33 \)) with a depth of \( 13.3 \, \text{cm} \). What is its apparent depth?
In a compound microscope, what limits the maximum magnification achievable with a single lens?

text_solutions: The maximum magnification of a single lens (simple microscope) is limited by its focal length. A shorter focal length increases magnification (m = 1 + D/f), but practical constraints like lens aberrations and the minimum focal length achievable restrict it to around 9-10x, necessitating a compound system.

qns_content.text: A concave lens of focal length \( 18 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 36 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 25 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification?

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 1.5 \, \text{cm} \) and tube length \( 18 \, \text{cm} \). If the eyepiece focal length is \( 6 \, \text{cm} \), what is the total magnification at infinity?

text_solutions:
Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{18}{1.5} = 12 \).

Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{6} \approx 4.17 \).

Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 12 \times 4.17 \approx 50 \).

qns_content.text: A telescope has an objective focal length of \( 150 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece focal length of \( 5 \, \text{cm} \). What is the length of the telescope tube?
A converging beam meets a convex lens (\( f = 12 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?
A prism of angle \( 30^\circ \) has a minimum deviation of \( 20^\circ \). What is the refractive index?
Why does a convex lens fail to form a sharp image when used with white light unless corrected?

text_solutions: A convex lens exhibits chromatic aberration with white light because different wavelengths refract by varying amounts due to the lens’s material having a wavelength-dependent refractive index. This causes colored fringes as focal points differ for each color, blurring the image.

qns_content.text: A ray of light passes from glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) to water (\( n = 1.33 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 50^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?

Why does a convex lens submerged in a liquid with the same refractive index as the lens not form an image?

options.text: Due to no refraction at the interfaces

text_solutions: When a convex lens is in a medium with the same refractive index, there is no difference in refractive indices between the lens and the medium. Without this difference, light does not bend at the interfaces, and the lens acts like a flat plate, failing to converge or diverge rays to form an image.

qns_content.text: A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.55 \) has radii of curvature \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -30 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 1.5 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 20 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?

text_solutions:
Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{20}{1.5} \approx 13.33 \).

Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{5} = 5 \).

Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 13.33 \times 5 \approx 66.65 \approx 67 \).

qns_content.text: A convex lens of power \( +4 \, \text{D} \) is used. What is its focal length?
A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.5 \) has radii of curvature \( 40 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -40 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?
In a convex lens submerged in a medium of higher refractive index, what happens to its ability to focus light?

text_solutions: When a convex lens is in a medium with a higher refractive index than the lens material, the refractive index difference reverses (medium > lens), causing the lens to diverge light instead of converging it. This occurs because the rays bend away from the normal at the interfaces.

qns_content.text: An object of height \( 2 \, \text{cm} \) is placed \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 5 \, \text{cm} \). What is the height of the image?
A ray of light passes from air (\( n = 1 \)) to water (\( n = 1.33 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 35^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
A concave lens has a focal length of \( 20 \, \text{cm} \). Where should an object be placed to get an image half the size of the object?

text_solutions:
Focal length: \( f = -20 \, \text{cm} \) (negative for concave lens).

Magnification: \( m = \frac{h'}{h} = 0.5 \) (virtual, diminished).

\( m = \frac{v}{u} \Rightarrow 0.5 = \frac{v}{u} \Rightarrow v = 0.5u \).

Lens formula: \( \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \).

\( \frac{1}{0.5u} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-20} \Rightarrow \frac{2}{u} - \frac{1}{u} = -\frac{1}{20} \).

\( \frac{1}{u} = -\frac{1}{20} \Rightarrow u = -20 \, \text{cm} \).

qns_content.text: What optical property of a prism allows it to be used in binoculars to invert images?

text_solutions: Prisms in binoculars use total internal reflection to invert and revert images. By reflecting light multiple times within the prism (e.g., in a Porro prism), the image orientation is corrected from the inverted form produced by the objective lens, maintaining the same size.

qns_content.text: A lens has a power of \( -3 \, \text{D} \). What is its focal length?

An object is placed \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) in front of a concave mirror of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \). Where is the image formed?
What happens to light rays when they strike a convex mirror at an angle parallel to its principal axis?

options.text: They reflect back along the same path
They appear to diverge from the focal point behind the mirror
They pass through the center of curvature

text_solutions: In a convex mirror, rays parallel to the principal axis diverge after reflection. When traced backward, these diverging rays appear to originate from the focal point behind the mirror, which is why the focal point is virtual and located on the opposite side of the incident light.

text_solutions:
Focal length: \( f = -10 \, \text{cm} \) (concave mirror).

Image distance: \( v = -20 \, \text{cm} \) (real image, same side as object).

Mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \).

\( \frac{1}{-20} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-10} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{-10} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{-2 + 1}{20} = \frac{-1}{20} \).

\( u = -20 \, \text{cm} \).

In a concave mirror, what prevents the formation of an image when the object is placed at the focal point?

options.text: Parallel reflected rays forming image at infinity

text_solutions: When the object is at the focal point of a concave mirror, the reflected rays become parallel and do not converge to a point. This results in the image being formed at infinity, meaning no distinct image forms at a finite distance.

qns_content.text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 180 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 6 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
Why does a prism disperse white light into a spectrum of colors?

options.text: Due to equal refraction of all wavelengths
Due to different refractive indices for different wavelengths
Due to reflection at the prism surfaces

text_solutions: A prism disperses white light because different wavelengths (colors) of light have different refractive indices in the prism material. Shorter wavelengths (e.g., violet) refract more than longer wavelengths (e.g., red), causing the light to split into a spectrum as it exits the prism.

qns_content.text: A convex mirror of focal length \( 18 \, \text{cm} \) produces an image \( 6 \, \text{cm} \) behind the mirror. What is the object distance?
What characteristic of a convex mirror makes it suitable for use as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?

options.text: Provides a wide field of view with a diminished image
Produces an inverted image for better clarity

text_solutions: A convex mirror always produces a virtual, erect, and diminished image, regardless of the object’s position. This provides a wide field of view, allowing drivers to see a larger area behind the vehicle, making it ideal for rear-view mirrors despite the reduced image size.

qns_content.text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 120 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 4 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
An object is at a depth of \( 16 \, \text{cm} \) in water (\( n = 1.33 \)). What is the apparent depth?
What is the primary reason optical fibers are bent without losing light transmission efficiency?

text_solutions: Optical fibers maintain light transmission when bent because the angle of incidence at the core-cladding interface remains greater than the critical angle, ensuring total internal reflection. This allows light to follow the bend without escaping into the cladding.

qns_content.text: A ray of light passes from glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) to air at an angle of incidence of \( 40^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
In a convex lens, why does the image transition from virtual to real as the object moves from inside to outside the focal point?

options.text: Due to change from divergence to convergence

text_solutions: Inside the focal point, a convex lens diverges rays, forming a virtual image on the same side. Beyond the focal point, the lens converges rays to a point on the opposite side, forming a real image. This transition occurs as the object crosses the focal point, changing the ray behavior.

qns_content.text: In a prism, what condition results in the minimum deviation of light?

options.text: Angle of incidence equals angle of emergence
Angle of incidence equals the prism angle

text_solutions: In a prism, minimum deviation occurs when the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence. This symmetry ensures the refracted ray inside the prism is parallel to the base, minimizing the deviation angle.

qns_content.text: A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 200 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
A ray of light passes from glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) to air at an angle of incidence equal to the critical angle. What is the angle of refraction?

text_solutions:
Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{1}{1.62} \approx 0.617 \).

\( i_c = \sin^{-1}(0.617) \approx 38.1^\circ \).

At critical angle, angle of refraction = \( 90^\circ \).

qns_content.text: Why does a reflecting telescope often use a secondary mirror in its design?

text_solutions: In a reflecting telescope (e.g., Cassegrain design), a secondary mirror redirects the light focused by the primary concave mirror through a hole in the primary mirror to the eyepiece. This allows a compact design with a long focal length, improving magnification and convenience of observation.

qns_content.text: A concave lens of focal length \( 25 \, \text{cm} \) has an object placed \( 50 \, \text{cm} \) from it. What is the image distance?
A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.5 \) has radii of curvature \( 15 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -15 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?
In a convex mirror, what is the significance of the focal point being behind the mirror?

options.text: It is the point where diverging rays appear to originate

text_solutions: The focal point of a convex mirror is virtual and behind the mirror because reflected rays diverge and appear to originate from this point when traced backward. This indicates the mirror’s diverging nature, ensuring all images are virtual, erect, and diminished.

qns_content.text: What is the key optical principle behind the working of a periscope?

text_solutions: A periscope uses total internal reflection in prisms (or plane mirror reflection) to redirect light. Prisms reflect light internally at angles greater than the critical angle, allowing the viewer to see objects from a different height or direction without direct line-of-sight.

Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{15}{1} = 15 \).

Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{5} = 5 \).

Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 15 \times 5 = 75 \).

A telescope has an objective of focal length \( 140 \, \text{cm} \) and an eyepiece of focal length \( 7 \, \text{cm} \). What is its magnifying power?
What is the primary optical phenomenon responsible for the mirage effect observed on hot roads?

text_solutions: The mirage effect on hot roads results from total internal reflection. Hot air near the ground has a lower refractive index than cooler air above, causing light from the sky to bend upward when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, creating an illusion of water.

qns_content.text: A ray of light passes from air (\( n = 1 \)) to glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 40^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
What is the significance of the critical angle in the context of total internal reflection?

options.text: It determines the focal length of a lens
It indicates the maximum angle of refraction
It defines the minimum angle for dispersion
It is the threshold for total internal reflection

text_solutions: The critical angle is the angle of incidence above which total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a rarer medium. At this angle, the refracted ray grazes the boundary (angle of refraction = 90°), and beyond it, all light is reflected back, enabling applications like optical fibers.

qns_content.text: What is the critical angle for a diamond (\( n = 2.42 \)) to glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) interface?
A ray of light passes from glass (\( n = 1.52 \)) to air at an angle of incidence of \( 45^\circ \). What happens?

text_solutions:
Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{1}{1.52} \approx 0.658 \Rightarrow i_c \approx 41.1^\circ \).

Since \( i = 45^\circ > i_c \), total internal reflection occurs.

qns_content.text: A prism of angle \( 60^\circ \) has a refractive index of \( 1.4 \). What is the angle of minimum deviation?
In a concave mirror, under what condition is the image formed virtual and magnified?

text_solutions: For a concave mirror, a virtual and magnified image is formed when the object is placed between the focal point (F) and the pole (P). Here, the reflected rays diverge, and their backward extensions converge behind the mirror, producing a virtual, erect, and magnified image.

qns_content.text: In a refracting telescope, why does the objective lens have a larger aperture than the eyepiece?

text_solutions: The objective lens in a refracting telescope has a larger aperture to collect more light from distant objects, enhancing brightness and resolution. The eyepiece, with a smaller aperture, magnifies this image, requiring less light-gathering capacity for viewing.

qns_content.text: A convex lens (\( f = 30 \, \text{cm} \)) and a concave lens (\( f = 15 \, \text{cm} \)) are in contact. What is the effective focal length?
In a plane mirror, why does the image distance equal the object distance?

options.text: Due to light converging behind the mirror
Due to equal angles of incidence and reflection

text_solutions: In a plane mirror, light reflects such that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. This symmetry ensures that the perpendicular distance from the object to the mirror equals the apparent distance of the image behind it, as the image forms along the normal extended backward.

qns_content.text: A prism of angle \( 40^\circ \) and refractive index \( 1.5 \) produces what minimum deviation?
An object at a depth of \( 19.95 \, \text{cm} \) in water (\( n = 1.33 \)) is viewed normally. What is the apparent depth?
In a plane mirror, what property ensures that the image is not distorted?

text_solutions: The flat surface of a plane mirror ensures that all incident rays reflect with equal angles of incidence and reflection, maintaining the object’s proportions and shape. Curved surfaces would distort the image by altering ray directions unevenly.

qns_content.text: What is the primary advantage of using a combination of lenses in optical instruments like microscopes?

options.text: Eliminates the need for a light source

text_solutions: A combination of lenses allows for greater magnification and improved image quality. The objective lens forms an initial image, which the eyepiece magnifies further, while multiple lenses can correct aberrations (e.g., chromatic, spherical), enhancing sharpness and clarity.

qns_content.text: A lens has a power of \( +2.5 \, \text{D} \). What is its focal length in centimeters?
Why does a convex lens produce chromatic aberration when used with white light?

text_solutions: Chromatic aberration occurs in a convex lens because different wavelengths of white light refract by different amounts due to the lens material’s varying refractive index for each wavelength. Shorter wavelengths (e.g., blue) focus closer than longer ones (e.g., red), causing color fringing.

qns_content.text: Why does a concave mirror used in a reflecting telescope require precise curvature?

options.text: To ensure rays converge to a single point

text_solutions: The precise curvature of a concave mirror ensures that all parallel rays from a distant object converge accurately to a single focal point. Any deviation in curvature causes spherical aberration, blurring the image and reducing the telescope’s resolving power.

qns_content.text: A simple microscope with a focal length of \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 25 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification?
An object is at a depth of \( 13.3 \, \text{cm} \) in a medium with refractive index \( 1.33 \). What is the apparent depth?
A concave mirror of radius of curvature \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) from the mirror. What is the object distance?
A ray of light passes from water (\( n = 1.33 \)) to air at an angle of incidence of \( 50^\circ \). What happens?

text_solutions:
Critical angle: \( \sin i_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{1}{1.33} \approx 0.752 \Rightarrow i_c \approx 48.75^\circ \).

Since \( i = 50^\circ > i_c \), total internal reflection occurs.

qns_content.text: An object of height \( 3 \, \text{cm} \) is placed \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) from a concave mirror of focal length \( 15 \, \text{cm} \). What is the height of the image?
An object is placed \( 12 \, \text{cm} \) from a convex mirror of focal length \( 18 \, \text{cm} \). What is the image distance?
A prism of angle \( 50^\circ \) and refractive index \( 1.4 \) produces what minimum deviation?

A compound microscope has an objective of focal length \( 1 \, \text{cm} \) and eyepiece of focal length \( 4 \, \text{cm} \) with a tube length of \( 14 \, \text{cm} \). What is the magnification at infinity?

text_solutions:
Objective magnification: \( m_o = \frac{L}{f_o} = \frac{14}{1} = 14 \).

Eyepiece magnification: \( m_e = \frac{D}{f_e} = \frac{25}{4} = 6.25 \).

Total magnification: \( m = m_o \times m_e = 14 \times 6.25 = 87.5 \).

qns_content.text: A light ray passes from water (\( n = 1.33 \)) to glass (\( n = 1.5 \)) at an angle of incidence of \( 30^\circ \). What is the angle of refraction?
What is the critical angle for a dense flint glass (\( n = 1.62 \)) to air interface?
A concave lens of focal length \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image \( 8 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?
A convex lens of focal length \( 10 \, \text{cm} \) forms an image at \( 20 \, \text{cm} \) from the lens. What is the object distance?
A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of \( 40 \, \text{cm} \). An object of height \( 2 \, \text{cm} \) is placed \( 30 \, \text{cm} \) in front of it. What is the height of the image formed?

text_solutions:
Focal length: \( f = \frac{R}{2} = \frac{-40}{2} = -20 \, \text{cm} \) (negative for concave mirror).

Object distance: \( u = -30 \, \text{cm} \).

Using mirror equation: \( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} \).

\( \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-30} = \frac{1}{-20} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{-20} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{-3 + 2}{60} = \frac{-1}{60} \).

\( v = -60 \, \text{cm} \) (real image).

Magnification: \( m = -\frac{v}{u} = -\frac{-60}{-30} = -2 \).

Image height: \( h' = m \times h = -2 \times 2 = -4 \, \text{cm} \) (inverted, so negative).

Magnitude of height = \( 4 \, \text{cm} \).

qns_content.text: An object is at a depth of \( 26.6 \, \text{cm} \) in a medium with refractive index \( 1.33 \). What is the apparent depth?
A converging beam meets a convex lens (\( f = 10 \, \text{cm} \)) \( 5 \, \text{cm} \) before the convergence point. What is the new image distance?
In a prism, when light is incident at a very small angle, what is the approximate relationship between deviation and the prism’s properties?

text_solutions: For a thin prism with a small angle of incidence, the deviation is approximately equal to the product of the prism’s refractive index minus one and the prism angle (D ≈ (n - 1)A). This simplification holds because the angles of refraction are small, minimizing higher-order effects.

In a concave mirror, when the object is placed at the center of curvature, where is the image formed?

options.text: Between focal point and center of curvature

text_solutions: For a concave mirror, when the object is at the center of curvature (C), the reflected rays converge back to the same point after reflection. This results in a real, inverted image formed at the center of curvature, with the same size as the object.

qns_content.text: In a compound microscope, what role does the eyepiece play in the final image formation?

options.text: Inverts the image to make it erect

text_solutions: The eyepiece in a compound microscope acts as a magnifying lens, taking the real, inverted image formed by the objective and producing a larger, virtual image for the observer. It enhances the angular size of the intermediate image, making it appear magnified without altering its orientation.

qns_content.text: In a concave lens, what property of the lens determines the position of the virtual focal point?

text_solutions: The virtual focal point of a concave lens is where diverging rays appear to originate when traced backward. This position is determined by the lens’s focal length, which depends on its curvature and refractive index, defining the extent of divergence.

qns_content.text: A double convex lens of refractive index \( 1.55 \) has radii of curvature \( 22 \, \text{cm} \) and \( -22 \, \text{cm} \). What is its focal length?
In a convex lens, what happens to the image if the object is placed between the focal point and twice the focal length?

text_solutions: For a convex lens, when the object is between the focal point (F) and twice the focal length (2F), the image is real, inverted, and magnified. It forms beyond 2F on the opposite side, as the rays converge after refraction.

Why does the image in a reflecting telescope remain free of chromatic aberration?

options.text: Due to uniform reflection of all wavelengths

text_solutions: A reflecting telescope uses mirrors instead of lenses as the objective. Mirrors reflect all wavelengths of light uniformly, avoiding the wavelength-dependent refraction that causes chromatic aberration in lenses, resulting in a clearer, color-corrected image.
